newsitem.title: USA: Dollar climbs as Japanese officials remain silent.
newsitem.headline: Dollar climbs as Japanese officials remain silent.

text.p: NEW YORK, Dec 30 - The dollar rose against the yen Monday amid a sudden lack of public pressure from Japanese officials trying to hold up the value of the Japense currency.

After the dollar had climbed above 115 yen Thursday, a senior official from Japan's Ministry of Finance had warned that Japanese monetary authorities do not welcome wild fluctuations in foreign exchange rates. A Bank of Japan official had also said the central bank was carefully monitoring developments in the foreign exchange market.
Since then, the dollar has repeatedly surged above 116 yen, but neither finance ministry or central bank officials have made any objections.
The dollar hit 116.20 yen Friday, its highest level in more than three-and-a half years, and nearly scaled that peak again Monday.
"Part of it is the fact that no Japanese official voiced any kind of concern about the dollar being higher overnight," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"In a sense, it seems that perhaps maybe the weak economy is forcing the Japanese goverment to back down from its 115 perceived ceiling."

Japan's struggling economy has benefited from a depreciating yen, which improves the competitiveness of Japanese exports such as automobiles. On the other hand, Japanese manufacturers located in the United States could suffer with American companies as the dollar continues to strengthen against the yen.
In late U.S. trading Monday, the dollar settled at 116.15 yen, up from 115.30 yen on Friday. The dollar rose slightly to 1.5550 German marks from 1.5545 marks.
Further dollar gains vs. the yen are possible if monetary officials in both Japan or the United States remain silent.

"If we don't have that type of comment or maybe even just an implied comment like that from either side, I think the dollar's definitely got some room to go higher," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank.
Dix said the only factor holding the dollar back is expected government opposition on either side of the Pacific to a stronger dollar.
A lingering slump in Tokyo stocks also helped boost the dollar relative to the yen Monday.

Tokyo's Nikkei index of 225 stocks finished the last trading day of the year at 19,361.35, down 7.69 points from Friday's close. Financial markets in Japan will resume trading Jan. 6 after the New Year holiday.
"The weak Nikkei, it's a real problem because the banks value their capital based on the stock prices because they own a lot of equity," Gilmore said.
"It undermines the fiscal position(s) of the institutions and the industry, and that's not a good sign," said Gilmore, adding it will keep pressure on Japanese interest rates.
Rock-bottom Japanese rates hurt the yen by making deposits denominated in that currency less attractive to investors.

Trading was light Monday ahead of the New Years holiday Wednesday. Most U.S. financial markets close early Tuesday and will remain closed until Thursday. Some European markets will close Tuesday as well as Wednesday.
Elsewhere, the British pound fell to $1.6920 Monday from $1.6945 Friday. The dollar climbed modestly to 1.3495 Swiss francs from 1.3485 francs, and strengthened to Canadian $1.3697 from C$1.3677.
